ref: Leg. 10 (Otto p.46; ANF ch.10, Pratten; Dods ch.10 at ANCL p.385)
greek: τοῦ θεοῦ λόγος τοῦ πατρὸς ἐν ἰδέα καὶ ἐνεργείᾳ· πρὸς αὐτοῦ γὰρ καὶ δι᾽ αὐτοῦ πάντα ἐγένετο, ἑνὸς ὄντος τοῦ πατρὸς καὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ.
greek_edition: Otto, Corpus Apologetarum Christianorum vol. VII (Jena: Mauke, 1857; Sändig reprint Wiesbaden 1969), archive.org item corpusapologeta02unkngoog; read from page image (PDF p.131) and OCR text layer; printed Otto spelling 'ἰδέα' (brief has ἰδέᾳ)
english: But the Son of God is the Logos of the Father, in idea and in operation; for after the pattern of Him and by Him were all things made, the Father and the Son being one.
translator: B. P. Pratten (ANF vol. 2) for the quoted English; Dods (ANCL vol. 2) differs only slightly
edition: Otto 1857/1969; ANF vol. 2 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Co., 1885); ANCL vol. 2 (Edinburgh: T. & T. Clark, 1867) p.385
what_it_says: The Son is the Father's Logos in idea and operation, and all things were made through him, the Father and the Son being one.
limits: 'ἑνὸς ὄντος' is read by Otto as Father and Son being one; Gesner's emendation ἑνὸς μὲν ὄντος is rejected by Otto. The phrase 'ἐν ἰδέα καὶ ἐνεργείᾳ' is an ideal/real principle (Otto's note 8: ideales und reales Princip), not an account of hypostases. Opponents (Arian/Sabellian readers) take 'Logos in idea' as a non-personal Logos.

ref: Leg. 10 (Otto p.46 n.9; ANF ch.10; Dods p.385)
greek: Ὄντος δὲ τοῦ υἱοῦ ἐν πατρὶ καὶ πατρὸς ἐν υἱῷ, ἑνότητι καὶ δυνάμει πνεύματος, νοῦς καὶ λόγος τοῦ πατρὸς ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ.
greek_edition: Otto vol. VII 1857 (archive.org corpusapologeta02unkngoog), page image PDF p.131 checked visually
english: And, the Son being in the Father and the Father in the Son, in oneness and power of spirit, the understanding and reason (νοῦς καὶ λόγος) of the Father is the Son of God.
page: Otto p.46 (Greek); Otto n.9 on p.46
what_it_says: The Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son, by oneness and power of the Spirit, and the Father's mind and reason is the Son of God.
limits: Otto's note 9 (p.46): here 'πνεύματος' is not the person of the Holy Spirit but the spiritual essence (divinitas) of Father and Son (cites Clericus 1716, Maranus, Dorner 1845 p.210). Read as a person it would be a Trinitarian text; read as Otto reads it, it is about the divine nature. Otto also records Venema's/Clarisse's doubts about 'νοῦς καὶ λόγος' (Venema conjectured πατὴρ νοῦς καὶ λόγος; Clarisse: no emendation needed).

greek: πρῶτον γέννημα εἶναι τῷ πατρί, οὐχ ὡς γενόμενον (ἐξ ἀρχῆς γὰρ ὁ θεός, νοῦς ἀΐδιος ὤν, εἶχεν αὐτὸς ἐν ἑαυτῷ τὸν λόγον, ἀϊδίως λογικὸς ὤν), ἀλλ᾽ ὡς τῶν ὑλικῶν ξυμπάντων, ἀποίου φύσεως καὶ γῆς ἀχρείας ὑποκειμένων δίκην, μεμιγμένων τῶν παχυμερεστέρων πρὸς τὰ κουφύτερα ἐπ᾽ αὐτοῖς, ἰδέα καὶ ἐνέργεια εἶναι προελθών.
greek_edition: Otto vol. VII 1857, PDF p.131 (image); sentence runs p.46 into p.47 (Latin page); some letters from OCR (κουφύτερα, ἀϊδίως spelling)
english: ...the first product of the Father, not as having been brought into existence (for from the beginning, God, who is the eternal mind [νοῦς], had the Logos in Himself, being from eternity instinct with Logos [λογικός]); but inasmuch as He came forth to be the idea and energizing power of all material things, which lay like a nature without attributes, and an inactive earth, the grosser particles being mixed up with the lighter.
translator: B. P. Pratten (ANF vol. 2); Dods (ANCL vol. 2, 1867, p.385) gives the same sense
what_it_says: The Son is the Father's first product, not as something made but as having come forth to be the idea and energy of matter, while God has the Logos eternally in himself.
limits: Otto's note 12 (p.47): 'προελθών' (came forth) distinguished from γενόμενον (made); Otto attributes the 'came forth' reading to Fabricius' conjecture προεῖλ- rejected; Otto says 'Noli mutare'. Opponents (Arian) take 'πρῶτον γέννημα' with 'came forth' as proof of a creature; the text itself says it is not as made. Not shown: the eternal/temporal relation of προβολή to the Logos is not explicitly defined.

ref: Leg. 10 (Otto p.48 with n.13; ANF ch.10 citing Prov. 8:22)
greek: Κύριος γάρ, φησίν, ἔκτισέ με ἀρχὴν ὁδῶν αὐτοῦ εἰς ἔργα αὐτοῦ.
greek_edition: Otto vol. VII 1857, PDF p.133 image checked; LXX/Prov. 8:22 cited by Otto n.13 (codd. edd. αὐτοῦ vs αὑτοῦ; Mon. ἔκτισέν με)
english: The Lord, it says, made me, the beginning of His ways to His works.
translator: B. P. Pratten (ANF vol. 2); Dods (ANCL vol. 2, p.386)
what_it_says: The prophetic Spirit says the Lord created him (the Logos) as the beginning of his ways.
limits: Otto's note 13: Athenagoras reads Prov. 8:22 of the Logos (as Justin does); Venema argued the Fathers referred it to the Spirit, and Otto rejects this. Otto notes 'ἔκτισέ με' is the reading of the text. The verb ἔκτισέ ('created') is the Arian proof-text; Athenagoras here frames it as the Logos being 'the first product', not made (see A3-03).

greek: Καίτοι καὶ αὐτὸ τὸ ἐνεργοῦν τοῖς ἐκφωνοῦσι προφητικῶς ἅγιον πνεῦμα ἀπόῤῥοιαν εἶναί φαμεν τοῦ θεοῦ, ἀποῤῥέον καὶ ἐπαναφερόμενον ὡς ἀκτῖνα ἡλίου.
greek_edition: Otto vol. VII 1857, PDF p.133 image checked; Otto n.14: Bodl. 1-2 and Aet. read καὶ ἀπόῤῥοιαν; Lübeck reads different order ἀπόῤῥοιαν φαμὲν τοῦ θεοῦ εἶναι
english: The Holy Spirit Himself also, which operates in the prophets, we assert to be an effluence of God, flowing from Him, and returning back again like a beam of the sun.
translator: B. P. Pratten (ANF vol. 2); Dods (ANCL vol. 2, p.386): 'an effluence of God, flowing from Him and returning back again like a beam of the sun'
what_it_says: The Holy Spirit, which works in the prophets, is an effluence of God that flows out and returns like a sunbeam.
use: objection (Spirit is only a power/emanation) | supports (Spirit is God's own)
limits: ἀπόῤῥοια is an image of emanation and return; the sentence does not call the Spirit a person (ὑπόστασις) and uses no 'hypostasis' or 'person' term. Its return-image is the Modalist (Sabellian) pattern, which opponents cite. Trinitarian readers say the Spirit is named among the three in A3-06 and 'of God'. Otto's note 14 variant reading is not decisive.

ref: Leg. 10 (Otto p.48; ANF ch.10 'Father, Son and Holy Spirit')
greek: Τίς οὖν οὐκ ἂν ἀπορήσαι, λέγοντας θεὸν πατέρα καὶ υἱὸν θεὸν καὶ πνεῦμα ἅγιον, δεικνύντας αὐτῶν καὶ τὴν ἐν τῇ ἑνώσει δύναμιν καὶ τὴν ἐν τῇ τάξει διαίρεσιν, ἀκούσας ἀθέους καλουμένους;
greek_edition: Otto vol. VII 1857, PDF p.133 image checked; Otto n.16 (Dorner, Daetzsch variants), n.17 Mon. θεούς for ἀθέους
english: Who, then, would not be astonished to hear men who speak of God the Father, and of God the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and who declare both their power in union and their distinction in order, called atheists?
translator: B. P. Pratten (ANF vol. 2); Dods (ANCL vol. 2, p.386) renders ἑνότης/τάξις similarly
what_it_says: Men who speak of God the Father, God the Son and the Holy Spirit, showing their power in union and distinction in order, are called atheists, which is unreasonable.
limits: Athenagoras names the three as θεός (two times) and πνεῦμα ἅγιον but gives 'union' as power (δύναμις) and 'distinction' as order (τάξις), not as hypostases; Otto (n.16) says the three are distinct by order yet equal by divinity, citing Athenagoras ch.24. No 'Trinity' word (τριάς) and no homoousios. Opponents (Unitarians) read 'ἐν τῇ τάξει' as subordination; defenders (Bull, Newman) as order of origin.

ref: Leg. 10 end (Otto pp.48-50; ANF ch.10 end)
greek: Καὶ οὐκ ἐπὶ τούτοις τὸ θεολογικὸν ἡμῶν ἵσταται μέρος· ἀλλὰ καὶ πλῆθος ἀγγέλων καὶ λειτουργῶν φαμεν, οὓς ὁ ποιητὴς καὶ δημιουργὸς θεὸς διὰ τοῦ παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ λόγου διένειμέ τε καὶ διέταξε περί τε τὰ στοιχεῖα εἶναι καὶ τοὺς οὐρανοὺς καὶ τὸν κόσμον καὶ τὰ ἐν αὐτῷ καὶ τὴν τούτων εὐταξίαν.
greek_edition: Otto vol. VII 1857; sentence runs p.48 (PDF 133) into p.50 (PDF 135); both checked visually; Otto n.19 'ἀγγ. καὶ λειτ.' = angeli et quidem ministri
english: Nor is our teaching in what relates to the divine nature confined to these points; but we recognise also a multitude of angels and ministers, whom God the Maker and Framer of the world distributed and appointed to their several posts by His Logos, to occupy themselves about the elements, and the heavens, and the world, and the things in it, and the goodly ordering of them all.
translator: B. P. Pratten (ANF vol. 2); Dods (ANCL vol. 2, p.386)
what_it_says: Beyond the Father, Son and Spirit the Christian doctrine of God also includes angels and ministers God made through his Logos.
limits: Otto's note 19: θεολογικόν here means the part of doctrine about the divine (numen); the angels are 'ministers' (λειτουργοί) distributed by God through the Logos. This is the lead-in to Leg. 24; it does not itself describe a hierarchy of worship.

greek: Εἰ δὲ ἀκριβῶς διέξειμι τὸν καθ᾽ ἡμᾶς λόγον, μὴ θαυμάσητε· ἵνα γὰρ μὴ τῇ κοινῇ καὶ ἀλόγῳ συναποφέρησθε γνώμῃ, ἔχητε δὲ τἀληθὲς εἰδέναι, ἀκριβολογοῦμαι· ἐπεὶ καὶ δὲ αὐτῶν τῶν δογμάτων οἷς προσέχομεν, οὐκ ἀνθρωπικοῖς οὖσιν ἀλλὰ θεοφάτοις καὶ θεοδιδάκτοις, πεῖσαι ὑμᾶς μὴ ὡς περὶ ἀθέων ἔχειν δυνάμεθα.
greek_edition: Otto vol. VII 1857, PDF p.135 image checked visually (confirmed 'πεῖσαι ὑμᾶς μὴ ὡς περὶ ἀθέων ἔχειν δυνάμεθα')
english: For presenting the opinions themselves to which we adhere, as being not human but uttered and taught by God, we shall be able to persuade you not to think of us as atheists.
translator: B. P. Pratten (ANF vol. 2) (the ANF sentence begins 'For presenting...' and is the end of the ch.10-11 bridge)
what_it_says: Athenagoras says he will set out the Christian teaching exactly, since it is God-taught, so that the reader will stop thinking Christians atheists.
limits: Otto's note 3 (p.51 Latin): δόγματα here are moral precepts (vivendi praecepta), distinct from doctrinal fides in ch.10; so the 'doctrines' of ch.11 are ethical teachings, not a creed. This matters for the Trinity reading: the Trinity passages are in ch.10 and 12, not in the ethics.

greek: Ἐπιτρέψατε ἐνταῦθα τοῦ λόγου ἐξακούστου μετὰ πολλῆς κραυγῆς γεγονότος ἐπὶ παρρησίαν ἀναγαγεῖν, ὡς ἐπὶ βασιλέων φιλοσόφων ἀπολογούμενον.
greek_edition: Otto vol. VII 1857, PDF p.135 image; word ἐξακούστου read from image/OCR (OCR also gave ἐξαπούστον); verify in print
english: Allow me here to lift up my voice boldly in loud and audible outcry, pleading as I do before philosophic princes.
what_it_says: Athenagoras asks the emperors to let him speak boldly as one pleading before philosopher-kings.
limits: Addressed to Marcus Aurelius and Commodus (the emperors). Not doctrinal; included for the setting of the ethics passage.

ref: Leg. 11 (Otto p.50 with n.5; ANF ch.11, citing Luke 6:27-28; Matt 5:44-45)
greek: Λέγω ὑμῖν· ἀγαπᾶτε τοὺς ἐχθροὺς ὑμῶν, εὐλογεῖτε τοὺς καταρωμένους, προσεύχεσθε ὑπὲρ τῶν διωκόντων ὑμᾶς, ὅπως γένησθε υἱοὶ τοῦ πατρὸς ὑμῶν τοῦ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς, ὃς τὸν ἥλιον αὐτοῦ ἀνατέλλει ἐπὶ πονηροὺς καὶ ἀγαθοὺς καὶ βρέχει ἐπὶ δικαίους καὶ ἀδίκους.
greek_edition: Otto vol. VII 1857, PDF p.135 image checked; Otto n.5 cites Luc. 6:27-28, Matth. 5:44-45
english: I say unto you, Love your enemies; bless them that curse you; pray for them that persecute you; that you may be the sons of your Father who is in heaven, who causes His sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the just and the unjust.
what_it_says: Christians are taught to love enemies, so that they may be sons of their heavenly Father.
use: context (ethics; Father-Son language in the moral, not metaphysical, sense)
limits: Sonship here is adoptive and moral, not the Son of ch.10. This is a gospel citation (Matthew/Luke, Otto n.5), not a statement about the Trinity.

greek: Ἆρα τοίνυν, εἰ μὴ ἐφεστηκέναι θεὸν τῷ τῶν ἀνθρώπων γένει νομίζομεν, οὕτως ἂν ἑαυτοὺς ἐξεκαθαίρομεν; Οὐκ ἔστιν εἰπεῖν. Ἀλλ᾽ ἐπεὶ πεπείσμεθα ὑφέξειν παντὸς τοῦ ἐνταῦθα βίου λόγον τῷ πεποιηκότι καὶ ἡμᾶς καὶ τὸν κόσμον θεῷ, διὰ τοῦτο τὸν μέτριον καὶ φιλάνθρωπον καὶ εὐκαταφρόνητον βίον αἱρούμεθα.
greek_edition: Otto vol. VII 1857, PDF p.149 (page 54) image checked; some letters OCR-level (τοίνυν, ἐφεστηκέναι)
english: Should we, then, unless we believed that a God presides over the human race, thus purge ourselves from evil? Most certainly not. But, because we are persuaded that we shall give an account of everything in the present life to God, who made us and the world, we adopt a temperate and benevolent and generally despised method of life,
what_it_says: Christians believe God presides over humankind and will judge their lives, so they choose a moderate, benevolent life.
use: context (one God as Maker and Judge; no Trinity in the sentence)
limits: Ch.12 has no 'one God' creed formula (the brief's 'we believe in the One God' is not in ch.12; the one-God sentences are in ch.4 and ch.7, outside this assignment). God is here singular 'θεός' (with the Maker). No Son or Spirit in this sentence.

ref: Leg. 12 (Otto p.54 with n.13, continuing to p.56; ANF ch.12, citing John 17:3 in Otto n.13)
greek: ὑπὸ μόνου δὲ παραπεμπόμενοι τοῦ τὸν θεὸν καὶ τὸν παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ λόγον εἰδέναι
greek_edition: Otto vol. VII 1857, p.54 (PDF 149) and p.56 (PDF 159) image checked; p.55 is the facing Latin page (Greek pages are even in this volume). TEXTUAL CRUX: Otto's apparatus on p.56 gives lemma 'ὑπὸ μόνου τοῦ εἰδέναι τὸν θεόν' with codd. and editions 'τούτου ὃν ἴσως θεόν'; Gesner proposed τούτου ὃν ἐπιθυμοῦσι; Struss proposed a conjecture at n.14. Printed text read as τοῦ τὸν θεόν; not settled from the image
english: ...who are conducted to the future life by this one thing alone, that they know God and His Logos,
what_it_says: Those who are led to the future life by this one thing, knowing God and his Logos (the Son), are pious.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (God and the Logos named together as the object of knowledge) | context (eternal life)
limits: Otto's n.13 cites John 17:3 as the source of the allusion ('this is eternal life, that they know thee...'); Athenagoras does not name Jesus. The crux means the exact phrase is not secure; a dual or plural reading (τούτου ὃν ἴσως θεόν) would change the sense. Opponents read 'ὁ λόγος' here as a creature; the text does not say.

ref: Leg. 12 (Otto p.56; ANF ch.12 'oneness of the Son with the Father...')
greek: τίς ἡ τοῦ παιδὸς πρὸς τὸν πατέρα ἑνότης, τίς ἡ τοῦ πατρὸς πρὸς τὸν υἱὸν κοινωνία, τί τὸ πνεῦμα, τίς ἡ τῶν τοσούτων ἕνωσις καὶ διαίρεσις ἐνουμένων, τοῦ πνεύματος τοῦ παιδὸς τοῦ πατρός,
greek_edition: Otto vol. VII 1857, PDF p.159 (page 56) image checked at 300 dpi; OCR gave ἔνρυμένων (image: ἐνουμένων); Otto n.15 Bodl.2 τί for τίς; n.16 κοινωνία (Bodl.1-2) vs κοινωνίας (Aet.); n.17 Gesner τούτων/τῶν τριῶν
english: ...what is the oneness of the Son with the Father, what the communion of the Father with the Son, what is the Spirit, what is the unity of these three, the Spirit, the Son, the Father, and their distinction in unity;
what_it_says: Christians must come to know the oneness of Son with Father, the communion of Father with Son, what the Spirit is, and the unity and distinction of these three: Spirit, Son, Father.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (the three named with unity and distinction, Spirit listed among them)
limits: Posed as questions Christians must learn, not answered; no 'what is the Spirit' answer is given here. The list is in the genitive and ends 'τοῦ πνεύματος τοῦ παιδὸς τοῦ πατρός' (Spirit, Son, Father) in a reversed order. Otto n.17 cites Gesner's τῶν τριῶν reading (not adopted). This is the closest Legatio passage to a Triad, but it is an eschatological aspiration, not a doctrinal statement of co-equality.

ref: Leg. 12 (Otto p.56; ANF ch.12 eternal life)
greek: πολὺ δὲ καὶ κρείττονα ἢ εἰπεῖν λόγῳ τὸν ἐκδεχόμενον βίον εἰδότες, ἐὰν καθαροὶ ὄντες ἀπὸ παντὸς παραπεμφθῶμεν ἀδικήματος,
greek_edition: Otto vol. VII 1857, PDF p.159 image checked
english: and who know that the life for which we look is far better than can be described in words, provided we arrive at it pure from all wrong-doing;
what_it_says: Those who know the future life is far better than words can say, and who reach it pure from wrongdoing, are the ones the author commends.
limits: Eternal life is conditional on purity from wrongdoing here; the passage does not describe resurrection (that is De resurrectione).

ref: Leg. 12 (Otto p.54; ANF ch.12 Plato, Minos, Rhadamanthus)
greek: Πλάτων μὲν οὖν Μίνω καὶ Ῥαδάμανθυν δικάσειν καὶ κολάσειν τοὺς πονηροὺς ἔφη, ἡμεῖς δέ, κἂν Μίνως ἢ Ῥαδάμανθυς ἢ κἂν ὁ τούτων πατήρ, οὐδὲ τοῦτόν φαμεν διαφεύξεσθαι τὴν κρίσιν τοῦ θεοῦ.
greek_edition: Otto vol. VII 1857, PDF p.149 (page 54) image read; some letters OCR-level (Ῥαδάμανθυν, κἂν)
english: Plato indeed has said that Minos and Rhadamanthus will judge and punish the wicked; but we say that, even if a man be Minos or Rhadamanthus himself, or their father, even he will not escape the judgment of God.
what_it_says: Plato's judges of the dead are subordinate to the one judgment of God, which none escapes.
limits: Plato (Gorgias 523-524) cited by Otto n.7. Single judge God; no Son or Spirit in the judgment.
